items.title: Hitler nearly walked out of the Nazi Party in 1921
items.claim: In July 1921, Hitler threatened to resign from the NSDAP unless he was given dictatorial control. What happened?

options.text: He was expelled and founded a rival party
The committee accepted his terms by a vote of 543 to 1 — the lone dissenter being a printer named Posch
He was forced to share leadership with Anton Drexler
The party split in two, with Hitler taking the Munich faction

items.reveal:
Anton Drexler had founded the German Workers' Party in 1919. Hitler joined in September 1919 as member 555 (the numbering started at 500 to inflate membership). By 1921 he was the party's most effective speaker.

When Drexler tried to merge with another nationalist group, Hitler resigned in protest, then demanded the chairmanship with dictatorial powers as the price of returning. The 29 July 1921 vote went 543 to 1.
items.why: Hitler's rise feels inevitable in hindsight. In 1921 he was a fringe agitator in a fringe party negotiating his way to control of an organisation with no national presence. Contingency, again.

items.title: The 14-year-old Richard II rode out to meet the rebels at Smithfield
items.claim: On 15 June 1381 the Peasants' Revolt ended at Smithfield. What actually happened?

options.text: The king's army defeated the rebels in open battle
Wat Tyler was killed by William Walworth, mayor of London, and Richard II rode forward and persuaded the crowd he would be their new leader
The rebels stormed the Tower of London and forced Richard to abdicate
John of Gaunt negotiated a settlement that gave rebels permanent rights

items.reveal_title: A teenage king and a dead leader
items.reveal:
Walworth stabbed Tyler during a parley. As Tyler fell, Richard II — aged 14 — rode forward and said 'You shall have no captain but me'. The rebels dispersed.

The charters Richard granted were revoked within weeks. John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered in July. Richard reportedly told a later petition: 'Villeins ye are, and villeins ye shall remain.' The poll tax was nonetheless quietly dropped.
items.why: Successful revolts are rare and brief. The 1381 rising failed in its immediate aims but ended the experiment with poll taxes for 600 years — until 1990.

items.title: The NHS opened on 5 July 1948 — over GP opposition
items.claim: Did the medical profession support the founding of the NHS?

options.text: Yes, the BMA welcomed it unanimously
No — most GPs initially opposed it, fearing loss of independence; Aneurin Bevan, Minister of Health, said he had 'stuffed their mouths with gold' by allowing private practice within the NHS

items.reveal:
A 1948 BMA poll found around 90% of doctors opposed to entering the NHS. Bevan negotiated: GPs would be self-employed contractors, not salaried employees; consultants could have NHS posts plus private patients; teaching hospitals retained boards.

The Beveridge Report (1942) had set out the framework — slaying the 'five giants' of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. The Labour government (1945-1951) implemented the welfare state. The NHS launched on 5 July 1948, the same day as National Insurance and the National Assistance Act.

Bevan resigned in 1951 over the introduction of prescription charges for dental and optical services.
items.why: Major institutions are rarely born from consensus. The NHS as a 'national treasure' obscures its messy founding — contested, negotiated, and quickly amended.
